cake-or-cupcake-peanut-butter.title: Cake or Cupcake with Peanut Butter

content.title: About
content.content: A cake or cupcake with peanut butter is a baked treat where a lightly sweetened, tender crumb is paired with the rich, nutty flavor of peanut butter. It works well for celebrations or everyday indulgence, offering a pleasant balance of sweetness and savory depth.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Peanut butter has been used in American cooking for over a century, famously in the classic PB&J sandwich.
Peanut‑butter cakes are often topped with chocolate ganache, caramel drizzle, or crushed peanuts for extra texture.
The oil in peanut butter helps keep the cake moist and extends its freshness.
In some regions, peanut‑butter cupcakes are a traditional fall‑time dessert.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Peanut butter provides monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Good source of plant protein
items.content: Two tablespoons (~32 g) deliver about 8 g of protein, aiding muscle repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: May help regulate blood sugar
items.content: The healthy fats slow carbohydrate absorption from the cake, helping to stabilize glucose levels.

items.title: Provides essential minerals
items.content: Peanut butter supplies magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium, important for nerve and muscle function.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanuts are a major allergen; reactions can be severe for sensitive individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Peanut butter is calorie‑rich (~190 kcal per 2 Tbsp), so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salted varieties add extra sodium; opting for unsalted versions is healthier.

items.title: Aflatoxin risk
items.content: Poorly processed peanut butter may contain aflatoxins, a toxin produced by mold. Choose reputable brands.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cake or cupcake as a standalone dessert, slice into portions, and garnish with fresh berries, fruit sauce, or a sprinkle of chopped peanuts. It also works well as a base for parfait‑style desserts layered with whipped cream or yogurt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the finished cake or cupcakes in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage (up to 1 week) refrigerate. Freeze in a sealed bag if you need to keep them for several months.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn flakes are a dry cereal product made from whole corn kernels that are steamed, rolled, and toasted to a crisp texture. The flavored version contains added taste enhancers, sugar, and sometimes vitamins, making it a popular breakfast choice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial corn flakes brand appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
Corn flakes are often used as a base for dessert bars and granola mixes.
Flavored flakes may contain natural or artificial flavorings; the exact composition is listed on the label.
Corn is one of the most cultivated grain crops worldwide, with production exceeding 1 billion tonnes per year.
Flakes readily absorb milk, creating a soft yet crunchy texture.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Corn flakes provide complex carbohydrates that quickly supply energy after breakfast.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Compared with many other cereals, flakes typically contain little fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Vitamin enrichment
items.content: Most manufacturers fortify flakes with B‑vitamins, iron, and sometimes vitamin D, enhancing their nutritional profile.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Thermal processing makes corn flakes easy to digest, which is convenient for children and older adults.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Although lower than whole grains, flakes still provide a modest amount of dietary fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Flavored flakes often contain added sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The product may contain milk, soy, or nut‑derived flavorings that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn flakes have a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid spikes in blood glucose levels.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Artificial flavors and preservatives may be undesirable for those seeking a clean‑label diet.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Flakes are typically served with milk or a plant‑based beverage; you can add fresh berries, banana slices, or nuts to boost nutritional value. They are also used in cooking: as a base for dessert layers, in breading, or in homemade snack bars.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cereal in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer to an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption and preserve crunchiness.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken wings are the small sections of a chicken's wing, typically fried, baked, or grilled. They are a popular snack, often served with sauces and seasonings. Wings have a crispy exterior and a juicy, flavorful meat inside.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wings are often called a "bar snack" in American cuisine, especially on pub menus.
The classic "Buffalo wings" originated in 1964 at the Anchor Bar in Buffalo, New York.
Wings come in different parts: the drumette and the flat (or wing tip).
There are countless sauces: from the classic hot sauce and butter blend to honey‑mustard, BBQ, and Asian soy‑ginger varieties.
Chicken wings are traditionally served with celery, carrot sticks, and blue‑cheese dressing.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken wings provide high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain niacin (B3), vitamin B6 and B12, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Wings supply iron, zinc and selenium, important for immune health and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: For low‑carb diets, wings offer a protein source without significant sugar content.

items.title: Collagen content
items.content: The skin and connective tissue are rich in collagen, which may benefit joint and skin health.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Wings are often prepared with oil or breading, increasing calories and saturated fat.

items.title: Salt and sauces
items.content: Sauced or salted versions can be high in sodium, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked wings may harbor salmonella; they should be cooked to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may have an allergic reaction to chicken proteins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wings are usually served hot as an appetizer. Eat them with your hands, pulling the meat off the bone, and dip in sauce. They pair well with celery, carrot sticks, and blue‑cheese dressing. Wings can also be added to salads, tacos, or used in Asian‑style dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh raw wings keep in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen wings last up to 9 months in the freezer. Thaw frozen wings in the fridge before cooking, and store cooked, cooled wings in an airtight container in the fridge for no more than 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee latte with non‑dairy milk is a classic espresso‑based drink diluted with hot plant‑based milk (soy, almond, oat, etc.). It offers a smooth, creamy taste while being suitable for those with lactose intolerance and vegans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Latte comes from the Italian word “latte” meaning “milk”.
The first latte recipe was recorded in the United States in the early 20th century.
Plant‑based milks reduce the carbon footprint of the drink compared with cow’s milk.
In many cafés latte is served with vanilla, caramel or cinnamon flavorings.
Caffeine content in a latte depends on the espresso shots, typically 60‑80 mg.

items.title: Energizing effect
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving alertness and reducing fatigue.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee provides polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Plant milks contain no lactose, making the drink safe for people with lactase deficiency.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Depending on the type of plant milk, the latte can be fortified with calcium, vitamin D and B12.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine may boost metabolic rate and aid calorie burning.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia or rapid heartbeat after caffeine.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened lattes can contain high amounts of added sugar, increasing calorie load.

items.title: Allergy to plant milk
items.content: Soy, almond or other plant milks may trigger allergic reactions in susceptible people.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can increase stomach acidity, which may be problematic for gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Latte is served hot in ceramic cups, often topped with foam, cinnamon or cocoa powder. Syrups (vanilla, caramel) or sweeteners can be added to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared latte is best consumed immediately. If stored, keep it in a sealed thermos in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Plant milk should be kept in its original container in the fridge, respecting the expiration date on the label.

double-cheeseburger-on-white-bun-2-mediu.title: Double Cheeseburger on White Bun, 2 Medium Patties

content.title: About
content.content: The double cheeseburger consists of two medium beef patties, melted cheese, fresh vegetables and sauce, placed between a split white bun. It is a classic fast‑food item popular worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first cheeseburger appeared in the United States in the 1920s, and the double version became popular in the 1970s.
White buns usually contain more sugar and fat than whole‑grain buns, making them softer and sweeter.
The combination of beef and cheese provides a high amount of protein and calcium in a single serving.
In some restaurants the double cheeseburger is served with a double layer of sauce, raising its calorie count to 800‑900 kcal.
Traditional American cheeseburger sauce often includes mayonnaise, ketchup, mustard and spices.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef patties provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The cheese adds calcium, supporting bone and dental health.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: Red meat is a good source of iron and zinc, important for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef and cheese supply B12, B6 and niacin, which help energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: Its high calorie content provides a quick energy boost, useful during intense physical activity.

items.title: High calories and saturated fat
items.content: The large amount of saturated fat and calories can contribute to weight gain if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salt in sauces and cheese raises sodium levels, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Potential meat pathogens
items.content: Undercooked patties may contain bacteria; they should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The burger is typically eaten by hand, holding it by the bun. It can be served with fries, additional sauces, or extra fresh vegetables according to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A prepared burger can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, keep components separate: patties and cheese in an airtight container, bun in a separate bag to prevent sogginess.

content.title: About
content.content: Lychee is a juicy tropical fruit native to Southeast Asia. It is covered by a thin, slightly rough brown skin that hides a translucent, sweet flesh with a rose‑like aroma and a hint of pear. The fruit is usually eaten fresh, but it is also used in desserts, drinks, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lychee belongs to the Sapindaceae family and is related to rambutan and durian.
In China lychee has been cultivated for over 2,000 years and was once called the “fruit of the emperor.”
The seeds contain toxic cyanogenic compounds and are not edible.
Several cultivars differ in size and sweetness, such as “Mise” and “Fosho.”
In some cultures lychee is considered a symbol of good luck and prosperity.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One fruit provides more than 70 % of the daily vitamin C requirement, supporting immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Flavonoids and anthocyanins in lychee help combat free radicals and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium contributes to normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber in the flesh promotes intestinal motility and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Provides copper and iron
items.content: These trace minerals are involved in hemoglobin formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to lychee, such as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Toxic seeds
items.content: The seeds and inedible parts contain cyanogenic glycosides and must not be consumed.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Lychee is relatively sweet, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Gastrointestinal issues
items.content: Large amounts can cause stomach upset due to the high fructose concentration.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peel the skin, remove the seed, and eat the flesh fresh. Lychee is added to fruit salads, smoothies, ice cream, and cocktails. It can also be made into jam, jelly, or a sauce for fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store lychee in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze the peeled flesh in bags—it retains flavor and aroma for up to 6 months.

stuffed-chicken-drumstick-or-breast-puer.title: Stuffed chicken, drumstick or breast, Puerto Rican style

content.title: About
content.content: A traditional Puerto Rican dish featuring chicken breast, drumstick or thigh that is stuffed with a fragrant mixture of vegetables, spices and sometimes cheese. The chicken is baked until a golden crust forms while staying juicy inside. The flavor profile combines sweet pineapple, tangy adobo and aromatic cilantro.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In Puerto Rico the dish is often served at holidays and family celebrations.
The stuffing may include mango, pineapple or sweet bell pepper, giving it a characteristic tropical taste.
A classic adobo marinade—garlic, oregano, vinegar and spices—is used to flavor the chicken.
It is commonly accompanied by rice and beans (arroz con gandules) and fried plantains.
Using the breast makes the dish leaner, while the drumstick stays especially moist.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat (especially breast)
items.content: Skinless breast meat contains very little saturated fat, supporting heart‑healthy eating.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is a good source of niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, which aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Adobo, garlic and oregano are rich in polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Fiber from vegetable stuffing
items.content: Added vegetables like peppers, onions and pineapple increase dietary fiber, promoting digestion.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in the sauce
items.content: Adobo marinades often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Undercooking risk
items.content: Chicken must reach an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F) to avoid food‑borne illness.

items.title: Natural sugars from fruit stuffing
items.content: Pineapple or mango add natural sugars, which may affect blood glucose control in diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, sliced into portions. It pairs well with rice, beans, fried plantains or a fresh salad. Leftovers can be used as a filling for tacos or sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers within two hours of cooking and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags for up to 2 months. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches 74 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Green iced tea in a bottle is a refreshing, calorie‑free beverage made from green tea leaves that are extracted, sweetened with non‑caloric sweeteners, and chilled. The diet version contains no added sugar, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green tea is rich in polyphenols, especially catechins, which have strong antioxidant properties.
The first commercial iced tea appeared in Japan in the early 1920s.
Diet versions often use stevia or sucralose instead of sugar.
Bottle packaging protects the drink from light, preserving flavor and color.
In many countries iced tea is a traditional summer refresher.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Catechins help neutralize free radicals, supporting cellular health.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Green tea extracts may boost fat oxidation and aid weight management.

items.title: Improved focus
items.content: A modest amount of caffeine enhances alertness without strong stimulation.

items.title: Sugar‑free hydration
items.content: The diet version provides fluid without extra calories or glycemic spikes.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Regular consumption of green tea is linked to better lipid profiles.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Even small amounts of caffeine can cause anxiety or sleep disturbances in some individuals.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some people may experience discomfort from sucralose or acesulfame‑K.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Green tea extracts can enhance the effects of anticoagulant medications.

items.title: Storage concerns
items.content: Prolonged exposure to heat may cause the drink to lose aroma and become cloudy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the iced tea chilled; you may add a slice of lemon or a sprig of mint for extra flavor. Limit consumption to 2‑3 servings per day, considering the caffeine content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bottle refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C. After opening, consume within 3‑5 days. Do not freeze, as it can alter the beverage’s texture.
